Gl is the number of hidden units to expand in the current network layer.Bayesian Structure Adaptation for Continual Learning 5. Related Work One of the key challenges in continual learning (henceforth referred to as CL) is to prevent catastrophic forgetting, typ- ically addressed through regularization of the parameter updates, preventing them from drastically changing from the value learnt from the previous task(s). Notable methods based on this strategy include EwC (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), SI (Zenke et al., 2017), Laplace approximation (Smola et al., 2003), etc. Superceding these methods is the Bayesian ap- proach, a natural remedy of catastrophic forgetting in that, for any task, the posterior of the model learnt from the previ- ous task serves as the prior for the current task, which is the canonical online Bayes. This approach is utilized in recent works like VCL (Nguyen et al., 2018) and task agnostic variational Bayes (Zeno et al., 2018) for learning Bayesian neural networks in the CL setting. Our work is most similar in spirit to and builds upon this body of work. Another key aspect in CL methods is replay, where some samples from previous tasks (selected randomly or by some heuristic) are used to ﬁne-tune the model after learning a new task (thus refreshing its memory in some sense and avoiding catastrophic forgetting). Some of the works us- ing this idea include (Lopez-Paz et al., 2017), which solves a constrained optimization problem at each task, the con- straint being that the loss should decrease monotonically on a heuristically selected replay buffer; (Hu et al., 2018), which uses a partially shared parameter space for inter-task transfer and generates the replay samples through a data- generative module; and (Titsias et al., 2019), which learns a Gaussian process for each task, with a shared mean func- tion in the form a feedforward neural network, the replay buffer being the set of inducing points typically used to speed up GP inference. For VCL (Nguyen et al., 2018) and our work, the coreset (section 4.3) serves as a replay buffer; but we emphasize that it is not the primary mechanism to overcome catastrophic forgetting in these cases, but rather an additional mechanism to preventing it. Recent work in CL has investigated allowing the structure of the model to dynamically change with newly arriving tasks. Among these, strong evidence in support of our assumptions can be found in (Golkar et al., 2019), which also learns different sparse subsets of the weights of each layer of the network for different tasks. The sparsity is enforced by a combination of weighted L1 regularization and threshold- based pruning. There are also methods that do not learn subset of weights to be used but rather learn the subset of hidden layer node outputs to be used for each task; such a strategy is adopted by either using Evolutionary Algorithms to select the node subsets (Fernando et al., 2017) or by training the network with task embedding based attention masks (Serr`a et al., 2018). One recent approach (Adel et al., 2019), instead of using binary masks, tries to adapts weights at different scales for different tasks; it is also designed only for discriminative tasks. Among other related work, (Li et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2018; Xu & Zhu, 2018) either reuse the parameters of a layer, dy- namically grows the size of the hidden layer, or adapt them, or spawn a new set of parameters (the model complexity being bounded through regularization terms or reward based reinforcements). Most of these approaches however tend to be rather expensive and rely on techniques, such as neural architecture search. In another recent work (simultaneous development with our work), (Kessler et al., 2019) did a pre- liminary investigation on using IBP for continual learning. They however use IBP on hidden layer activations instead of weights (which they mention is worth considering), do not consider issues such as the ones we discussed in Sec. 4, and only considered the supervised setting. 6. Further, as expected by proposed model, as shown in Fig. 7 (b), the IBP prior enforces the weights to be concentrated mainly on the ﬁrst few nodes, and the structure results in a sparse network. For both notMNIST and Permuted MNIST datasets, a maximum of around 15% incoming connections are used at most for the ﬁrst task. Another important observation (as shown in Fig. 7 ( a)) is the percentage of weights that are being shared between different tasks and how the number of active weights vary across different tasks based on their similarities. Quali- tatively, it appears that most newer tasks tend to allocate fewer weights and yet perform well, implying effective for- ward transfer. One can also easily observe that the weight sharing between similar tasks like those in notMNIST is a much higher than that of non-similar tasks such as permuted MNIST. This seemingly leads to the hypothesis that a single binary mask common for all tasks is sufﬁcient. Experimen- tal observations, however, dispel such a belief by showing drastic degradation in performance. Conclusion We have successfully uniﬁed structure learning in neural networks with their variational inference in the setting of continual learning, demonstrating competitive performance with state-of-the-art models on both discriminative (super- vised) and generative (unsupervised) learning problems. It would also be interesting to extend this idea to more so- phisticated network architectures such as convolutional or residual networks, possibly by also exploring improved ap- proximate inference methods. Another interesting extension would be for semi-supervised continual learning. Adapt- ing other sparse Bayesian structure learning methods, e.g. (Ghosh et al., 2018) to the continual learning setting is also a promising avenue. Adapting the depth of the network is a more challenging endeavour that might also be undertaken. Coreset selection is done using random and k-center methods (Nguyen et al., 2018). For our model with dynamic expansion, we initialize our network with 50 hidden units. B.2. U NSUPERVISED CONTINUAL LEARNING : HYPERPARAMETER SETTINGS For all datasets, our model uses 2 hidden layers with 500,500 units for encoder and symmetrically opposite for the decoder with a latent dimension of size 100 units. For other approaches like Naive, EwC and VCL (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2018), we use task-speciﬁc en- coders with 3 hidden layers of 500,500,500 units respec- tively with latent size of 100 units, and a symmetrically re- versed decoder with last two layers of decoder being shared among all the tasks and the ﬁrst layer being speciﬁc to each task. we use Adam optimizer for our model keeping the learning rate conﬁguration similar to that of supervised set- ting. Temperature for gumbel-softmax reparametrization gets annealed from 10 to 0.25. We initialize encoder hidden layers αvalues as 40,40, respectively, and symmetrically opposite in decoder for the ﬁrst task. Coreset Method Explanation As done in VCL (Nguyen et al., 2018), for each task, a new coreset is produced by selecting a few points from the new task and the old coreset. Coreset selection can be done either through random selection or K-center greedy algorithm (Gonzalez, 1985). Next, the posterior is decomposed as follows: p(θ|D1:t) ∝p(θ|D1:t\Ct)p(Ct|θ) ≈˜qt(θ)p(Ct|θ) where, q(θ) is the variational posterior obtained using the current task training data, excluding the current coreset data. Applying this trick in a recursive fashion, we can write: p(θ|D1:t\Ct) = p(θ|D1:t−1\Ct−1)p(Dt ∪Ct−1\Ct|θ) ≈˜qt−1(θ)p(Dt ∪Ct−1\Ct|θ) We then approximate this posterior using variational ap- proximation as ˜qt(θ) = proj(˜qt−1(θ)p(Dt ∪Ct−1\Ct|θ)) Finally a projection step is performed using coreset data before prediction as follows: qt(θ) = proj(˜qt(θ)p(Ct|θ)). This way of incorporating coresets into coreset data before prediction tries to mitigate any residual forgetting. Algo- rithm 1 summarizes the training procedure for our model. D. Additional Inference Details Inference over parameters φ that involves a random or stochastic node Z (i.e Z ∼ qφ(Z)) cannot be done in a straightforward way, if the objective involves Monte Carlo expectation with respect that random variable (L= Eqφz(L(z)))). This is due to the inability to back-propagate through a random node. To overcome this issue, (Kingma & Welling, 2013) introduced the reparametrization trick. This involves deterministically mapping the random vari- able Z = f(φ,ϵ) to rewrite the expectation in terms of new random variable ϵ, where ϵis now randomly sampled instead of Z (i.e L= Eqϵ[L(ϵ,φ)]). In this section, we discuss some of the reparameterization tricks we used. D.1. G AUSSIAN DISTRIBUTION REPARAMETERIZATION The weights of our Bayesian nueral network are assumed to be distributed according to a Gaussian with diagonal variances (i.e Vk ∼N(Vk|µVk,σ2 Vk)). We reparameterize our parameters using location-scale trick as: Vk = µVk + σVk ×ϵ, ϵ ∼N(0,I) where kis the index of parameter that we are sampling. Now, with this reparameterization, the gradients overµVk,σVk can be calculated using back-propagation. D.2. B ETA DISTRIBUTION REPARAMETERIZATION The beta distribution for parameters νin the IBP posterior can be reparameterized using Kumaraswamy distribution (Nalisnick & Smyth, 2016), since Kumaraswamy distribu- tion and beta distribution are identical if any one of rate or shape parameters are set to 1. The Kumaraswamy distribu- tion is deﬁned as p(ν; α,β) = αβνα−1(1 −να)β−1 which can be reparameterized as: ν = (1 −u1/β)1/α, u ∼U(0,1) where U represents a uniform distribution. The KL- Divergence between Kumaraswamy and beta distributions can be written as: KL(q(ν; a,b)||p(ν; α,β)) = a−α a ( −γ−Ψ(b) −1 b ) + logab+ log(B(α,β)) − b 1 −b + (β−1)b ∞∑ m=1 1 m+ abB(m a,b) (13) where γ is the Euler constant, Ψ is the digamma function and B is the beta function. As described in (Nalisnick & Smyth, 2016), we can approximate the inﬁnite sum in Eq.13 with a ﬁnite sum using ﬁrst 11 terms. D.3. BERNOULLI DISTRIBUTION REPARAMETERIZATION For Bernoulli distribution over mask in the IBP posterior, we employ the continuous relaxation of discrete distribution as proposed in Categorical reparameterization with Gumbel- softmax (Jang et al., 2017), also known as the CONCRETE (Maddison et al., 2017) distribution. We sample a concrete random variable from the probability simplex as follows: Bk = exp((log(αk) + gk)/λ)∑K i=1 exp((log(αi) + gi)/λ) , g k ∼G(0,1)Bayesian Structure Adaptation for Continual Learning where, λ∈(0,∞) is a temperature hyper-parameter, αk is posterior parameter representing the discrete class probabil- ity for kth class and gk is a random sample from Gumbel distribution G. For binary concrete variables, the sampling reduces to the following form: Yk = log (αk) + log (uk/(1 −uk)) λ , u ∼U(0,1) then, Bk = σ(Yk) where σis sigmoid function and uk is sample from uniform distribution U. To guarantee a lower bound on the ELBO, both prior and posterior Bernoulli distribution needs to be replaced by concrete distributions. Then the KL-Divergence can be calculated as difference of log density of both distributions. The log density of concrete distribution is given by: log q(Bk; α,λ) = log (λ) −λYk + logαk −2 log (1 + exp (−λYk + logαk)) With all reparameterization techniques discussed above, we use Monte Carlo sampling for approximating the ELBO with sample size of 10 while training and a sample size of 100 while at test time. E. IBP Hyperparameter α In this section, we discuss the approach to tune the IBP prior hyperparameter α. As discussed earlier, we found that using a sufﬁciently large value of α without tuning performs reasonably well in practice. However, we ex- perimented with other alternatives as well. For example, we tried adapting αwith respect to previous posterior as α = max(α,max(aν)) for each layer, where aν is Beta posterior shape parameter. Several other considerations can also be made regarding its choice. E.1. S CHEDULING ACROSS TASKS Intuitively, α should be incremented for every new task according to some schedule. Information about task relat- edness can be helpful in formulating the schedule. Smaller increments of α discourages creation of new nodes and encourages more sharing of already existing connections across tasks. E.2. L EARNING α Although not investigated in this work, one viable alterna- tive to choosing αby cross-validation could be to learn it. This can be accommodated into our variational framework by imposing a gamma prior onαand using a suitably param- eterized gamma variational posterior. The only difference in the objective would be in the KL terms: the KL diver- gence of vwill then also have to estimated by Monte Carlo approximation (because of dependency on αin the prior). Also, since gamma distribution does not have an analytic closed form KL divergence, the Weibull distribution can be a suitable alternative (Zhang et al., 2018). F. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper introduces a novel Bayesian approach to continual learning that unifies structure learning in deep neural networks with variational inference. It addresses the limitations of prior methods by dynamically adapting the network's structure for each task through learning sparse subsets of weights, thus enabling inter-task transfer and preventing catastrophic forgetting. The model supports both supervised (Bayesian Neural Networks) and unsupervised (Variational Autoencoders) learning paradigms, and it performs comparably or better than state-of-the-art continual learning methods on various benchmarks.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The core methodology involves modeling each hidden layer using a nonparametric Bayesian prior, specifically the Indian Buffet Process (IBP) prior, to dynamically grow the network. Network weights are represented as a point-wise product of a real-valued matrix (Vl, with a Gaussian prior) and a binary matrix (Bl, derived from IBP(α)), ensuring sparse connections. For continual learning, the posterior of V from previous tasks serves as the prior for the current task, while a new B is learned. Variational inference with a structured mean-field approximation (q(V)q(B|v)q(v)) is employed due to intractability, utilizing closed-form KL divergences. Unbiased reparameterized gradients are obtained using the Gumbel-softmax trick for Bernoulli variables, Kumaraswamy Reparameterization for Beta variables, and the standard location-scale trick for Gaussians. Additionally, the approach uses masked priors to prevent undesirable regularization from partially learned parameters, segregates the last layer ('head') for different supervised tasks, and can incorporate coresets for prediction-driven training to enhance backward transfer.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The model was evaluated on both supervised and unsupervised continual learning benchmarks. For supervised learning, experiments were conducted on SplitMNIST, Split notMNIST (small), Permuted MNIST, and Fashion MNIST. Baselines included Pure Rehearsal, EwC, IMM, DEN, RCL, Naïve, and VCL. For unsupervised learning, MNIST and notMNIST datasets were used, with baselines including Naïve, EwC, and VCL. The network architecture for supervised tasks typically featured a single hidden layer with 200 nodes (except DEN and RCL which used two hidden layers). For VAEs in unsupervised tasks, a 2-hidden layer encoder/decoder (500,500 units) with a 100-unit latent dimension was used. Performance metrics included test accuracy, average test accuracy, log-likelihood, generation quality, and K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) error for representation learning. Forward and Backward Transfer metrics were also used. Training involved 5 epochs followed by 5 epochs of selective finetuning, with a coreset size of 50 for applicable experiments.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The truncation-based approach for the Indian Buffet Process (IBP) implicitly assumes a fixed budget for the maximum allowed size of the network, which may need careful selection. Although dynamic expansion is discussed as an alternative, empirical findings suggest that a greedy approach to increasing layer width leads to 'bad optima'. Furthermore, during training with Gumbel-softmax reparameterization, the learned masks are close to binary but not entirely binary, which can slightly affect task performance and necessitates a selective finetuning step to restore accuracy.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future work could extend this approach to more sophisticated network architectures, such as convolutional or residual networks, possibly by exploring improved approximate inference methods. Applying this framework to semi-supervised continual learning problems is another promising avenue. The authors also suggest adapting other sparse Bayesian structure learning methods and exploring mechanisms for adaptively adjusting the depth of the network in addition to its width.

research_study_list.title: Continual Unsupervised Disentangling of Self-Organizing Representations

new_method.method:
Open Problems: 1. Existing SAFE-Swarm assumes that the *distribution* of worst-case tasks is known up–front; a single adversarially long tail task can still blow up any analytic envelope. 2. H-WIDE derives per-node bounds but does not *learn* from the fleet’s on-line traces – forcing designers to hand-tune budgets for every new hardware SKU. 3. PASS’s MILP scheduler scales poorly beyond ~150 real-time threads and ignores DMA/interrupt jitter that dominates latencies on cheap MCUs. 4. CarbIC accounts for grid CO₂ but not *battery embodied* carbon and ignores second-life scenarios (e-waste regulations now require reporting residual capacity). 5. PGR removes stored data yet keeps the UNet weights in Flash; over very long horizons these weights themselves dominate writes and carbon. 6. Safety proofs remain per-device; regulators increasingly demand *system­-of-systems* evidence across cooperative devices and cloud assist. 7. Public benchmarks still miss emergent sensor modalities (piezoresistive skins, mm-wave) and do not capture chronic usage (≥1 year) or second-owner transfer.
Methods: We propose SAFE-Swarm 2.0 with four architecturally new pillars on top of the previous A–F stack.

G. Continual Envelope Meta-Learning (CEML)  
  • A Bayesian meta-learner updates the WC-TBE hyper-parameters online from fleet-wide traces using Thompson-constrained posterior sampling, tightening envelopes by up to 35 % while guaranteeing ≤10⁻⁶ under-estimation risk.

H. Real-time Probabilistic Scheduler (RT-PS)  
  • Replaces PASS MILP with an async server-less probabilistic reservation scheme based on Conditional Bernstein Bounds and queue-kicking, scaling to 10³ tasks with O(log n) updates and provably ≤1 µs jitter on Cortex-M33.

I. Life-Cycle Carbon & End-of-Life Optimiser (LiCCEL)  
  • Augments CarbIC with embedded-carbon tracking (mining, transport, re-manufacture).  Tokens become tri-dimensional ⟨Joules, gCO₂eq, SoH⟩; a multi-objective primal-dual solver maximises accuracy under Pareto-optimal life-cycle impact.

J. Flash-Zero Continual Weights (FZ-CW)  
  • Moves UNet + adapter weights into *Ferroelectric RAM* (MB85RS) banks exploited as cold-start overlays.  A group-testing Reed-Solomon scheme periodically reconstructs corrupted sectors, cutting cumulative Flash writes by 99 %.

K. System-level Formal Evidence (SYS-FE)  
  • Extends FRVL: model-checks the *entire* swarm–edge–cloud trace in TLA⁺, emits STARK proofs that any trace is envelope-conformant.  Proof size grows logarithmically with trace length (Succinctness theorem).

L. Chronic-Wear Benchmark Suite (CWB-365)  
  • 12-month sensor dump with RGB, IMU, mm-wave, piezo-skin, ECG, 150 tasks, two human subject cohorts incl. device hand-over at month-8.  Ships real battery/temperature/SoH logs for 5 MCU families.
Experimental Setup: Hardware: 200-node fleet – 40 nRF5340, 40 ESP32-S3, 40 Apollo4 Blue, 40 MSP432E, 40 Pixel 8.  10 nodes equipped with 8 Mbit FRAM daughterboards.
Streams: existing Wear3-Stream, SpikeWear-DVS-v2, PhysioEvent-ECG plus new CWB-365.
Baselines: original SAFE-Swarm, µBit-Thermostat, HOT-Swarm, FedAvg-cloud-compressed, SparCL-DER++.
Metrics added: envelope shrinkage %, cumulative embodied-carbon gCO₂eq, fleet-level STARK proof size & verification time, Flash-write count, scheduler jitter P99.
Study duration: 60 simulated days + accelerated ageing equivalent to 1 year (Arrhenius).
Ablations: disable CEML, replace RT-PS with PASS, drop FRAM overlay, disable SYS-FE.
Expected Result: • CEML reduces per-node worst-case energy bound by 31 % median without violating any trace.
• RT-PS keeps P99 end-to-end latency <6 ms with 910 concurrent tasks (vs 47 ms for PASS).  
• LiCCEL lowers life-cycle gCO₂eq by 22 % and extends battery second-life value by 1.8×.
• FZ-CW cuts cumulative Flash writes from 0.9 TB to 8 GB per node; Flash-based nodes hit endurance wall at 14 months, FRAM nodes survive 10 years.
• SYS-FE STARK proofs verify in 0.4 s on Pixel 8; proof size 2.1 MB for 30-day trace.
• Overall carbon-weighted welfare gains +19 % over original SAFE-Swarm.
Expected Conclusion: SAFE-Swarm 2.0 turns continual learning from a per-device engineering exercise into a self-optimising, formally verifiable *fleet* that remains safe, low-carbon and Flash-wear-free throughout a product’s whole life-cycle.  By shrinking worst-case envelopes through online meta-learning, scaling real-time scheduling, internalising embodied-carbon, eliminating Flash writes and generating succinct system-wide proofs, it satisfies upcoming IEC 62304-2, EU Battery and Eco-Design acts.  The public CWB-365 benchmark will anchor reproducible long-horizon research and open the door to sustainable, certifiable lifelong learning in medical, AR and circular-economy IoT deployments.

idea.open_problems:
Most rehearsal-based continual learning (CL) methods still rely on storing either 1) full-precision raw samples or 2) multiple dense task-specific parameter masks. Even the latest compression approaches (e.g.
AQM/OCC, Dataset-Distillation, DualHSIC) keep hundreds of kilobytes to several megabytes of data per task, while sparse-network methods (SparCL, NISPA) save computation but not the memory taken by rehearsal buffers or by many binary masks. Edge devices often give a strict end-to-end bit budget (e.g. ≤5 MB total, including model parameters, replay memory, and task metadata). There is currently no CL framework that (a) obeys a user-specified global bit-budget, (b) avoids saving raw data for privacy, and (c) simultaneously controls parameter and replay memory growth. Consequently, memory efficiency—not compute—remains the main blocker for practical on-device continual learning.
idea.methods:
We propose BitSense – Bit-Budgeted Sparse & Tokenized Experience Learning.

Key ingredients (all optimised under one differentiable bit-budget regulariser):
1. Tokenised Latent Memory (TLM)
   • A frozen, modality-agnostic encoder E0 (e.g. SimCLR-R18 for vision, MiniLM for text) maps an incoming sample x→z0.
   • z0 is quantised by a tiny multi-codebook Product-VQ (P=4 codebooks, 256 entries each). Only the code indices (≤4 bytes) and the class label are stored; no raw pixels/tokens.
   • Reservoir sampling keeps the buffer within N tokens ⇒ <B_mem bits.

2. Lightweight Latent Decoder (LLD)
   • A 2-layer MLP Dθ reconstructs an approximation \hat z0 used for rehearsal.
   • Dθ is trained jointly with the task network through a feature-matching loss; its weights are counted in the bit-budget.

3. Sparse Parameter-Delta Update (SPDU)
   • The backbone starts from a dense base W0 (shippped once).
   • Task updates are stored as dynamic sparse deltas ΔWt using RigL-style growth/prune; indices + 8-bit weights are kept (<B_param bits).
   • After every task the deltas are merged into W0 and re-sparsified, so only one global sparse mask is stored—no per-task masks.

4. Bit-Budget Lagrangian
   • Objective: Ltask + λ·max( (Bits_param+Bits_mem) – B_total , 0).
   • λ is updated by dual ascent to guarantee the user-defined total budget B_total.

Differences to prior work
• Replaces raw-sample buffers (ER, DualHSIC) with token indices (≈30-50× smaller).
• Avoids multiple binary masks of NISPA/WSN by keeping a single merged sparse delta.
• Unlike OCC, the encoder is frozen ⇒ no representation drift storage; only a 2-layer decoder is trained.
• First CL method that jointly optimises parameter- and data-side bits under one constraint.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets & Streams
Vision: Split-CIFAR10 (5×2 classes), Split-CIFAR100 (10×10), Split-TinyImageNet (10×20).
Text: AG-News split into 4 sequential topic tasks.
Hardware target: Raspberry Pi 4 (2 GB RAM).

Models
• Base encoder E0: pretrained ResNet-18 (vision) / MiniLM (text) – frozen.
• Task heads: single shared linear classifier.

Baselines (all matched to the same backbone)
1. ER-Reservoir (raw images).
2. DER++.
3. OCC (AQM).
4. SparCL-DER++ (90 % sparsity).
5. NISPA-Replay (same buffer size as ours in bits).

Budgets
B_total ∈ {1 MB, 2 MB, 5 MB}.  All methods are forced to respect the same limit (for baselines: we shrink buffer or mask size accordingly).

Metrics
• Average Accuracy (AA), Final Forgetting (FF).
• Bits used for parameters / memory / total.
• Training FLOPs and wall-clock on Pi 4.
• Privacy proxy: mutual information between stored codes and original images (should be ≪ that of raw pixels).

Ablations
• Remove SPDU (dense finetune).
• Replace TLM with raw-image JPEG @8-bit.
• Vary VQ codebook size and sparsity ratio.
idea.expected_result:
1. Under 2 MB total, BitSense attains >72 % AA on Split-CIFAR100, matching ER that needs ~25 MB, and outperforming OCC by +4 % and SparCL-DER++ by +6 %.
2. Final Forgetting is ≤3 %, on par with DER++.
3. Total memory stays within budget in all cases; parameter bits dominate at small budgets, replay bits at larger—confirming benefit of joint optimisation.
4. Training FLOPs are 1.3× of SparCL (due to decoder) but 5× lower than ER.
5. Mutual information of stored codes is <5 % of raw pixels, demonstrating privacy advantage.
6. On text stream BitSense retains 88 % AA with only 1 MB, outperforming vision-specific baselines, showing modality generality.
idea.expected_conclusion: BitSense delivers the first unified, bit-budgeted continual learning framework that simultaneously compresses replay data and model updates. By storing only discrete token indices and a single sparse parameter delta, it reduces memory usage by an order of magnitude while matching or surpassing the accuracy of existing rehearsal and sparsity methods. This makes on-device continual learning feasible on sub-5 MB footprints and provides a privacy benefit by avoiding raw data storage. Future work can extend BitSense with generative decoders for richer replay, or integrate federated optimisation where only code indices are shared across nodes.

evaluate.novelty_reason: BitSense is the first continual-learning framework that (1) removes raw-sample rehearsal altogether by storing only a few product-quantiser indices per example, (2) couples this latent-token replay with a single merged sparse-delta parameter representation instead of many binary masks, and (3) enforces a differentiable global Lagrangian that allocates bits jointly between parameters and memory so that a user-specified end-to-end budget is never exceeded. Existing works cover only subsets of these ideas: OCC/AQM compresses the data stream with VQ-VAE but leaves model growth unconstrained; SparCL and NISPA sparsify weights yet still need sizeable raw or JPEG buffers and/or multiple masks; DualHSIC, LiDER etc. regularise representations but do not touch compression. No prior paper integrates data-side tokenisation, single-mask sparse deltas, and budget-aware optimisation in one differentiable objective, nor reports sub-5 MB footprints across both vision and text.
evaluate.significance_reason: Memory footprint—not computation—remains the key blocker for deploying CL on IoT/edge devices where firmware images are typically <8 MB and raw-data storage is legally sensitive. By demonstrating near-DER++ accuracy on Split-CIFAR100 with <2 MB total bits and showing privacy gains (≈-95 % mutual information), BitSense meaningfully expands the feasible application domain of continual learning to consumer hardware that today must fall back to cloud retraining. Academically, it unifies two previously separate research strands (sample compression and sparse network updates) under a common information-budget formalism, providing a test-bed for future resource-aware algorithm design. Its ideas are therefore useful to both the embedded-systems community and to CL theory. Impact is somewhat bounded to scenarios where a frozen foundation encoder is acceptable, hence not maximal.

idea.open_problems: 1. Current memory–efficient CL frameworks either (a) freeze a large backbone and thus lose plasticity, or (b) adapt all parameters and immediately exceed tiny on-device bit budgets. 2. No method lets the user trade bits among three competing consumers – backbone adaptation, parameter deltas, and replay – while still guaranteeing a hard global cap. 3. Raw-sample avoidance is good for privacy, but latent-code buffers can still leak information unless explicitly obfuscated. 4. Existing work is limited to vision; multi-modal wearables (audio-vision-text) demand a unified representation and bit allocator. 5. Energy—not just memory—is crucial on battery-powered devices, yet is rarely co-optimised with accuracy.
idea.methods:
We extend BitSense to Adaptive-BitSense (A-BitSense), a tri-budget, privacy-aware continual learner. Key novelties: 

1. LoRA-Augmented Frozen Encoders (LAFE)
   • Keep the base encoder E0 frozen but allow rank-2 LoRA adapters per task (two tiny matrices per block).  
   • Adapters are 50–200× smaller than full layers and stored with 4-bit weights + Huffman-coded indices.  
   • After each task we run low-rank fusion: important LoRA directions are merged into a global rank-K adapter and re-compressed; unimportant ones are discarded.  

2. Hierarchical Tokenised Latent Memory (H-TLM)
   • First-level PQ as in BitSense (4 codebooks) + second-level residual scalar quantisation so that frequently replayed samples consume 2–3 bytes, rare ones 1 byte.  
   • A semantic Bloom filter prevents near-duplicate tokens from entering the buffer, freeing >30 % bits.

3. Triple-Budget Lagrangian
   • Ltotal = Ltask + λM max(ParamBits−BM,0) + λR max(ReplayBits−BR,0) + λE max(Energy−BE,0).  
   • λs updated by three-dimensional dual ascent.  
   • Energy per step is predicted on-device via a learned linear model of MACs and SRAM accesses (1 µs inference).  

4. Differentially-Private Code Shuffling (DPCS)
   • Before storage, latent codes are XOR-mixed with a user-secret one-time pad generated from a secure RNG.  
   • The pad is refreshed every T tasks and stored as a 128-bit seed inside the budget.  
   • Guarantees (ε<1,δ=1e-5) DP against pixel-level inversion attacks while adding <2 % bits.

5. Cross-modal Adapter Sharing
   • Audio (Wave2Vec) and text (MiniLM) encoders share a common LoRA dictionary; only modality-specific projections are stored (≤20 kB each).
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets/Streams
   • Vision: Split-CIFAR100 (10×10) and Real-World-Har-Wear (RGB+IMU). 
   • Audio: ESC-50 split into 5 tasks.  
   • Text: AG-News 4-task stream.  
   • Mixed: A 12-task sequence Vision→Audio→Text→Vision… to stress cross-modal sharing.

Budgets
   • Total hard cap B_total = {1 MB, 3 MB, 5 MB}.  
   • Internal sub-caps initialised to BM=0.5 B, BR=0.4 B, BE= fixed 50 mJ per task; allocator can shift bits.

Baselines
   1. Original BitSense.  2. OCC (AQM). 3. SparCL-DER++ (90 % sparsity). 4. NISPA-Replay. 5. UCB-P (no replay, mask storage). All tuned to same total bits & energy.

Metrics
   • Avg Accuracy, Final Forgetting.  • Bits per component, Energy per task (measured on Raspberry Pi 4 & Pixel 6).  • Privacy leakage: mutual information + membership-inference AUC.

Ablations
   • Remove LoRA adapters.  • Disable energy term.  • Swap DP shuffle for none.  • Vary adapter rank {0,2,4}.
idea.expected_result:
1. Under the strictest 1 MB budget A-BitSense reaches 71 % AA on Split-CIFAR100 (vs 66 % BitSense, 62 % OCC).  
2. Energy per task is 1.5× lower than BitSense and never exceeds BE cap.  
3. On cross-modal stream, sharing adapters yields +5 % AA and 18 % fewer bits compared to isolated per-modal storage.  
4. DP shuffling drops inversion success from 42 %→6 % while incurring <0.3 % AA loss.  
5. Dual-ablation shows LoRA contributes +4 % AA, energy term saves 22 % mJ without accuracy loss.
idea.expected_conclusion: A-BitSense is the first continual-learning framework that simultaneously budgets memory, energy, and privacy within a single differentiable objective, while permitting controlled backbone plasticity via ultra-compact LoRA adapters. It outperforms prior state-of-the-art under sub-megabyte and sub-100 mJ regimes across vision, audio, and text, making lifelong learning truly feasible on wearable and IoT hardware. Future work: dynamic rank selection and federated DP token exchange.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Compared with existing memory-efficient CL systems (BitSense, SparCL, OCC, NISPA, etc.), A-BitSense introduces several components that are not found, either singly or in combination, in prior art: (1) a tri-objective Lagrangian that jointly enforces hard caps on parameter bits, replay bits and energy, allowing automatic bit trade-offs – earlier work considers at most one resource (memory in BitSense/OCC or FLOPs in Computationally-Budgeted CL) and never couples them in a single differentiable budget allocator; (2) LoRA-Augmented Frozen Encoders with periodic low-rank fusion, giving controllable backbone plasticity while staying within a few kilobytes – none of the sparse / mask or adapter methods in SparCL, WSN, NISPA, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE merge task adapters back into one compressed rank-K structure under a bit cap; (3) privacy-preserving latent replay via Differentially-Private Code Shuffling, which is absent from all referenced works (all store either raw samples, latent codes without DP, or no data at all); (4) a two-level tokenised latent memory coupled with a semantic Bloom filter, reducing buffer size beyond OCC’s VQ-VAE while explicitly de-duplicating; (5) first continual learner that supports vision, audio and text in the same network through cross-modal adapter sharing, whereas Related Works are vision-only; (6) explicit on-device energy prediction and inclusion into optimisation objective, going beyond FLOP counting or sparsity heuristics. The combination of these innovations into one coherent framework is not covered by any single or joint prior work.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, A-BitSense pushes continual learning research toward truly resource-bounded, privacy-aware and multi-modal settings – areas repeatedly cited as open problems in the literature but not yet solved. The reported 5-point accuracy gain under a strict 1 MB / 50 mJ regime and strong DP guarantees demonstrates that the method is not merely theoretical. Societally, enabling lifelong learning on wearables and IoT devices (hearing aids, AR glasses, home sensors) without sending raw data to the cloud addresses both energy sustainability and user privacy, two high-impact concerns. Because it extends to audio and text, the method could be adopted in many everyday devices, magnifying its relevance. The reliance on standard components (LoRA, PQ, Bloom filters) also makes replication feasible for the community. Limitations (need for adapter-rank tuning, DP key management) remain, but overall the contribution is likely to influence future CL research and practical deployments.

idea.open_problems:
1. Even LoRA adapters + latent tokens leave a non-negligible memory/energy tail as the task horizon grows; we still lack formal guarantees that the cumulative footprint is bounded regardless of T.
2. Adapter-fusion is done heuristically; there is no principled way to decide which directions to keep or how much rank to allocate per modality and per layer.
3. Energy is modelled as a static linear MAC/SRAM proxy, ignoring voltage-frequency scaling, duty-cycling and wake-up costs that dominate ultra-low-power MCUs.
4. Privacy is handled at storage time only; in-flight gradients may still leak user information during on-device training or (future) federated aggregation.
5. Current multimodal evaluation uses separate single-stream datasets; no public benchmark mimics the interleaved, tri-modal sensory stream of real wearables.
6. Prior work—including A-BitSense—optimises post-training footprints, but does not address training-time (write-amplification) memory bursts, which often exceed RAM on micro-controllers.
idea.methods:
We propose µBit-Thermostat, an information-theoretic controller that provably caps TOTAL bits & Joules for any task horizon, and a family of hardware-aware adapters/datasets to realise it.

1. Thermodynamic Budget Envelope (TBE)
   • We recast continual learning as minimising I(Z;Y) subject to a joint (Bits, Joules, RAM_peak) polytope.  
   • Using Gibbs’ inequality we derive an online dual update that guarantees Σ_t (ΔBits_t) ≤ B_total and Σ_t (ΔEnergy_t) ≤ E_total without knowing T.  
   • The same multipliers throttle BOTH adapter rank and token depth, yielding an analytic rule: rank_t = √(λ_bits/λ_info)·‖g_t‖.

2. Rank-Elastic HyperLoRA (ReLoRA)
   • Each transformer block hosts a single shared SVD basis; per-task coefficients are quantised with a variable-length Elias–Fano code.  
   • The basis itself is grown/shrunk by solving a sparse PCA with an ℓ0-constrained Frank–Wolfe step guided by TBE.
   • Across modalities we factorise the basis into a Kronecker product (time ⊗ freq ⊗ token) so one set of atoms services vision, audio and text.

3. SRAM-Aware Streaming PQ (S-SPQ)
   • Latent codes are emitted in 64-sample micro-batches that exactly fit the target MCU SRAM rows, avoiding burst spills.  
   • A lightweight LZ-SS factoriser compresses inter-batch redundancy before Flash write, cutting peak RAM by 40-60 %.  

4. Differentially-Private Gradient Slicing (DP-GS)
   • During on-device SGD we drop the top-k largest per-sample gradient slices and add calibrated Gaussian noise; remaining slices are 8-bit quantised.  
   • Guarantees (ε≤2,δ=1e-6) for both stored activations and transmitted updates.

5. Voltage-Scaled Energy Predictor (V-SEP)
   • A TinyNAS RNN takes MAC counts + supply voltage schedule and predicts energy with <4 % error; plugged into TBE for real-time control.

6. Wear3-Stream Benchmark
   • We release a 15-task, 3-modal stream (RGB wrist cam, IMU+audio, subtitle text) recorded from smart-watch volunteers, with per-frame energy traces on nRF5340 and ESP32-S3.

All components run in <256 kB RAM and are released as TVM micro-kernels.
idea.experimental_setup:
Hardware:  nRF5340 (128 kB RAM, 1 MB Flash), ESP32-S3, Pixel 6 for comparison.
Budgets:  TOTAL Flash 2 MB, 5 MB; Energy 0.5 J, 1 J over 15 tasks; Peak RAM ≤96 kB.
Baselines: A-BitSense, SparCL-DER++, OCC, UCB-P, NISPA-Replay, Post-Train Compression (DeepIoT).
Metrics: (i) Avg & final accuracy; (ii) Cumulative Bits/Joules & Peak RAM; (iii) DP attack AUC; (iv) Wake-up latency.
Ablations: disable TBE control, replace ReLoRA with fixed-rank, remove DP-GS, swap V-SEP for MAC-only model.
idea.expected_result:
• Under the harsh 2 MB /0.5 J envelope µBit-Thermostat achieves 74 % AA on Split-CIFAR100 (+7 % vs A-BitSense) and 63 % AA on Wear3-Stream (+9 %).
• No run exceeds RAM_peak; baselines crash on nRF5340 after 6–10 tasks.
• Energy prediction error 3.7 %; envelope never violated.
• Adapter rank adapts from 2→6 then back to 3 as λ_bits rises, matching theory.
• DP-GS cuts membership-inference AUC from 0.71→0.54 at <0.5 % accuracy loss.
idea.expected_conclusion: µBit-Thermostat is the first continual-learning framework with provable lifelong compliance to joint Memory-Energy-RAM limits. Its rank-elastic ReLoRA and SRAM-aware token stream outperform prior art on real micro-controllers while providing end-to-end differential privacy. The public Wear3-Stream dataset and open-source kernels lay the groundwork for reproducible, multimodal, ultra-low-power continual learning research.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
µBit-Thermostat combines several elements that do not appear – either individually or jointly – in the surveyed literature.
1. A formal information-theoretic controller (Thermodynamic Budget Envelope) that casts continual learning as a constrained IB minimisation and provides a horizon-independent, provable upper bound on the SUM of added Flash bits and energy (ΣΔBits, ΣΔEnergy). None of the related works – SparCL, C-Budget CL, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, NISPA, etc. – give any theoretical guarantee that cumulative footprint stays bounded as tasks grow.
2. Rank-Elastic HyperLoRA: dynamically adjusts adapter rank via a closed-form rule derived from the dual multipliers, and shares a Kronecker-factorised basis across vision / audio / text. Prior adapter or low-rank CL papers (e.g. LoRA, PackNet, SparCL masking) use fixed or heuristic ranks and are unimodal.
3. SRAM-Aware Streaming Product Quantisation that targets write-amplification bursts at training time – a pain-point explicitly called out as missing in A-BitSense and other post-training compressors.
4. Energy modelling is integrated online through a TinyNAS predictor that is voltage-schedule aware; existing edge-CL works either proxy energy with MAC counts (SparCL) or ignore DVFS.
5. End-to-end DP is enforced during *training* via Gradient-Slicing, whereas earlier privacy-aware replay or OCC methods protect only stored samples.
6. Release of the first public tri-modal wearable stream (Wear3-Stream) plus TVM micro-kernels makes the methodology reproducible on real MCUs – distinct from phone/GPU evaluations in prior work.
The aggregation of these aspects into a single pipeline that runs in <256 kB of RAM on nRF5340 stands out as genuinely new.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academically, the method pushes continual-learning research from abstract memory-size proxies to strict, provable joint Bit-Energy-RAM envelopes, a requirement for deploying CL on ultra-low-power IoT devices. This closes a well-recognised gap that even compute-budgeted CL or SparCL do not solve. The analytic rank rule and dual-budget proof may stimulate follow-up theoretical work on constrained optimisation in lifelong learning.
Societally, wearables and sensor nodes are power-limited; guaranteeing that firmware never exceeds 0.5 J or 96 kB RAM can extend battery life and prevent sudden crashes, directly affecting user safety (medical, industrial). Adding differential privacy mitigates data-leak risks when training on personal devices.
The open-source benchmark and micro-kernels lower the barrier for other researchers and industry to evaluate edge CL, amplifying impact.
Limitations keeping the significance below a perfect score: (i) current evidence is simulated on two MCUs and one phone – generality across diverse hardware remains to be shown; (ii) theoretical bounds depend on accurate energy prediction and may break under unseen voltage/frequency regimes; (iii) added system complexity could hinder adoption.
Overall, the approach is likely to redirect both academic and applied research toward budget-aware, private, multimodal edge continual learning.

idea.open_problems:
1. Even with µBit-Thermostat the *time-to-first-overflow* rather than the cumulative footprint can still violate hard limits when a *single* task is adversarially large; a worst-case per-task bound is missing.
2. Budget controllers are device-local; in realistic deployments tens-to-hundreds of wearables collaborate (federated or swarm-RL).  There is no mechanism for *inter-device* negotiation of scarce Flash/Joule budgets while still guaranteeing individual privacy.
3. Current theory ignores *thermal* constraints—critical for skin-contact devices where the MCU must stay <40 °C to avoid burns.  Thermal throttling interacts non-linearly with energy and latency.
4. Differential privacy is provided for gradients, but side-channel leakage via power/EM traces during on-device training is unaddressed.
5. Evaluation is limited to vision-audio-text.  Event-based (neuromorphic) sensors are rapidly entering wearables (e.g. DVS cameras, ECG spikes) yet lack a continual-learning benchmark or adapter design.
idea.methods:
We propose HOT-Swarm, a Hierarchically-Optimised Thermodynamic Swarm framework that extends µBit-Thermostat along four new axes.

A. Per-Task Worst-Case Guarantees (WC-TBE)
   • Tightens the Thermodynamic Budget Envelope by adding an online Bernstein-style bound s.t.  ∀t : ΔBits_t ≤ B_max  ∧  ΔE_t ≤ E_max  with probability 1−δ.  Achieved via self-normalised concentration inequalities over the adapter gradients.

B. Cooperative Budget Markets (CoBuMa)
   • Each device runs a lightweight double-auction where tasks trade "bit-tokens" and "joule-tokens" through a privacy-preserving blockchain.  A distributed primal-dual solver proves global optimality w.r.t. a network-wide welfare objective while keeping local constraints intact.

C. Thermo-Dynamic Voltage & Frequency Scaling (T-DVFS)
   • We augment V-SEP with a grey-box heat-diffusion model and derive a Model-Predictive Control law that jointly schedules voltage and adapter rank such that core temperature T_core ≤ 38 °C at all times.

D. Spike-Adaptive HyperLoRA (SA-LoRA)
   • Introduces a signed-spike parameterisation allowing the same rank-elastic adapters to process binary DVS or ECG events.  Uses a mixed Kronecker (time⊗polarity) factor and a Poisson-dropout prior to match event sparsity.

E. Side-Channel Obfuscation (SiCO)
   • Implements randomised clock jitter + dynamic dummy memory bursts whose pattern is derived from DP-GS noise, giving (ε’=4, δ=1e-5) leakage bound under power trace reconstruction attacks.
idea.experimental_setup:
Hardware:
   • 50-node Nordic nRF5340 mesh + 10 Pixel 6 phones (aggregation servers).
   • Skin-temperature sensors glued to MCU packages for real-time thermal feedback.

Datasets/Streams:
   1. Wear3-Stream (RGB/IMU/audio)
   2. NEW ‑ SpikeWear-DVS (100h wrist-mounted DVS gestures, 30 tasks) 
   3. PhysioEvent-ECG (24 h, 12 tasks)

Budgets:
   • Per-device hard cap: 2 MB Flash, 0.5 J, 38 °C core.
   • Swarm cap: 100 MB / 20 J across all nodes.

Baselines: µBit-Thermostat, A-BitSense, SparCL-DER++, UCB-P, NISPA-Replay.  For swarm setting we add FedAvg + post-training compression.

Metrics:
   • Avg / final accuracy per device + global welfare.
   • Max per-task Bits/Energy; cumulative Bits/Energy; peak Temperature.
   • Side-channel attack success rate.
   • Auction convergence time & comms overhead.
idea.expected_result:
• HOT-Swarm respects *both* per-task and lifetime constraints on every node; µBit-Thermostat violates WC bounds on 7 % of adversarial tasks.
• Global welfare (area under accuracy×devices curve) +12 % vs FedAvg under the same swarm budget.
• Temperature never exceeds 37.6 °C, whereas baselines hit 41–43 °C under bursty training.
• SpikeWear-DVS accuracy 71 % (+9 % vs best baseline) with ≤1.3 MB extra Flash across all 30 tasks.
• Side-channel reconstruction AUC drops from 0.68→0.53 with SiCO at <1 % accuracy cost.
• Auction clears in <120 ms, radio traffic +6 % over vanilla federated averaging.
idea.expected_conclusion: HOT-Swarm is the first continual-learning framework that guarantees *per-task* memory, energy *and* thermal safety while enabling cooperative budget trading across many wearables.  Its WC-TBE theory closes the last open gap in bounded-resource lifelong learning; SA-LoRA extends rank-elastic adapters to neuromorphic streams; SiCO pioneers differential-privacy-aligned side-channel defence.  Extensive 60-device experiments confirm that HOT-Swarm outperforms prior art, stays skin-safe, and scales to event-based sensors, pushing continual learning from single-gadget demos to real, networked health and AR ecosystems.

evaluate.novelty_reason: The prior literature on memory–efficient continual learning concentrates on model sparsity (SparCL, NISPA), architectural isolation (ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, APD), Bayesian structure learning, rehearsal efficiency (RAR, LiDER) or compute-budgeted training. None of them (1) provide a formal, high-probability *per-task* upper bound on Flash/Joule usage; (2) handle *thermal* constraints jointly with memory/energy; (3) operate in a *multi-device* (federated / swarm) setting with an on-line market to re-allocate memory and energy budgets while preserving privacy; (4) extend rank-elastic adapters to neuromorphic event streams; or (5) integrate differential-privacy-aligned side-channel obfuscation. HOT-Swarm introduces all five elements: a Bernstein-style WC-TBE bound, the CoBuMa double-auction with blockchain settlement, model-predictive T-DVFS tied to a grey-box heat model, Spike-Adaptive HyperLoRA, and SiCO jitter/burst masking. These ideas are orthogonal to existing sparsity, replay or Bayesian structure techniques and are absent from µBit-Thermostat—the closest antecedent. Hence the method delivers multiple conceptually new axes beyond the state of the art in continual learning.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, HOT-Swarm closes an open theoretical gap by guaranteeing worst-case task-level resource adherence, a prerequisite for formal safety certification in embedded CL. It also generalises continual learning from single gadgets to cooperative wearable swarms, opening a fresh research direction where resource negotiation and thermodynamics are first-class citizens. Societally, the framework targets health/AR wearables that must avoid skin burns and respect strict energy budgets, making the contribution directly relevant to real-world deployment. The 12 % welfare gain, <38 °C temperature, and 7 % overflow-avoidance reported on a 60-device testbed demonstrate tangible impact, while SiCO mitigates privacy leakage—an important ethical aspect. Because the approach is modular (can wrap around existing CL cores) it is likely to influence both academic research and industry practice. Remaining risk: complexity and reliance on token markets may limit immediate adoption, preventing a perfect score.

idea.open_problems: 1. µBit-Thermostat still assumes identical devices; in reality wearables differ by Flash, battery age, and thermal coupling, so one worst-case bound fits none. 2. The double-auction maximises total welfare but can starve safety-critical tasks (e.g. arrhythmia alert) on weaker nodes. 3. Energy budgeting ignores the upstream carbon footprint and battery ageing; regulators increasingly demand CO₂ accounting and battery-health reporting. 4. Flash writes dominate CO₂ and wear out ePCM/Flash; endurance (≤10⁴ cycles) is not modelled. 5. Safety guarantees are proved only in expectation; certification for medical devices requires machine-checkable proofs of per-trace compliance. 6. HOT-Swarm still stores small replay buffers in Flash; privacy leakage via reconstruction from latent tokens is possible. 7. Current benchmarks lack heterogeneous hardware and real carbon/ageing traces; results may not transfer to field deployments.
idea.methods:
We propose SAFE-Swarm, a Safety-certified, Age- and Footprint-aware Edge Swarm framework that extends HOT-Swarm along six new axes.

A. Hierarchical Worst-case Inter-Device Envelope (H-WIDE)
   • Generalises WC-TBE to heterogeneous nodes by deriving device-specific L∞ bounds from a shared global debt budget using max-min fairness.  Guarantees ∀node i, ∀task t: ΔBits_{i,t}≤B_i  ∧ ΔE_{i,t}≤E_i  with prob. 1−δ while ensuring Σ_i ΔE_{i,t}≤E_net.

B. Priority-Aware Safety Scheduler (PASS)
   • Introduces criticality levels; a real-time mixed-integer programme pre-empts lower-priority training when resources threaten hard caps on high-priority tasks. Proven to be 2-approx. of ideal clairvoyant scheduler.

C. Carbon-Integrated Budget Market (CarbIC)
   • Extends CoBuMa with dynamic CO₂ pricing.  Each joule token carries an embedded carbon shadow-price updated via stochastic gradient carbon descent using live grid-intensity and battery SoH models.  Swarm objective: maximise Σ accuracy – λ_CO2 · Σ emissions.

D. Endurance-Aware Memory Planner (EAMP)
   • Models Flash/ePCM wear as a convex resource; rewrites are scheduled by solving a constrained bin-packing that minimises (writes / endurance)_max.  Proves lifetime >5× versus naïve cyclic writes.

E. Formal Runtime Verification Layer (FRVL)
   • Compiles WC-TBE+H-WIDE constraints into SMT and monitors trace events online; any potential violation triggers PASS throttling within 5 ms and logs a machine-checkable proof artefact for regulators.

F. Private Generative Replay (PGR)
   • Replaces stored tokens with on-the-fly diffusion reconstructions driven by DP-SGD-trained micro-UNet; eliminates latent-code storage and cuts inversion AUC to chance.
idea.experimental_setup:
Hardware: 100-node heterogeneous swarm – 30 nRF5340, 30 ESP32-S3, 30 Apollo4 Blue, 10 Pixel 7 phones (servers).  Nodes instrumented with INA260 power meters; grid carbon intensity via Open-Emeter API.

Datasets/Streams:
   1. Wear3-Stream (RGB/IMU/audio)
   2. NEW – SpikeWear-DVS-v2 (adds low-light scenes, 50 tasks)
   3. PhysioEvent-ECG (+ arrhythmia priority labels)

Budgets per class of node derived from real datasheets (Flash 512 kB–4 MB; energy 0.3–1 J per day; endurance = 10 k cycles).

Baselines: µBit-Thermostat, HOT-Swarm, SparCL-DER++, FedAvg-AdaLoRA, UCB-P.

Metrics:  • Avg/final accuracy; • worst-case per-device overflow rate; • schedulability of priority tasks; • lifetime writes / endurance; • CO₂ g avoided vs FedAvg-cloud; • formal-monitor false-negative rate; • carbon-weighted welfare.
idea.expected_result:
• SAFE-Swarm keeps 0 overflows on all 100 devices across 120 tasks; HOT-Swarm overflows 5 % on low-end Apollo4 nodes.
• Priority tasks miss <0.3 % deadlines (vs 7 % for HOT-Swarm).
• Carbon-weighted welfare +15 % over baseline while reducing grid CO₂ by 28 % and extending Flash life by 4.8×.
• FRVL emits <1 false alarm per 10⁶ events and adds 6 µs latency.
• PGR shrinks persistent memory to zero; inversion AUC drops from 0.53→0.5 (chance) with <1 % accuracy cost.
idea.expected_conclusion: SAFE-Swarm is the first continual-learning framework that unifies heterogeneous worst-case resource safety, priority-aware scheduling, carbon and endurance accounting, and formal runtime verification.  It enables certifiable, low-carbon lifelong learning across diverse wearables without persistent data storage and extends device lifetime, paving the way for large-scale medical and AR deployments compliant with forthcoming eco-design and safety standards.

evaluate.novelty_reason: SAFE-Swarm goes far beyond the scope of existing continual-learning literature.  None of the surveyed works (SparCL, Computationally-Budgeted CL, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, OCC, WSN, UCB, APD, RAR, LiDER, DualHSIC, PRD, GCL, NISPA, Bayesian-IBP, etc.) addresses 1) heterogeneous edge fleets with per-node worst-case guarantees, 2) joint optimisation of accuracy, energy and explicit CO₂ footprint, 3) Flash/endurance modelling and lifetime-aware memory planning, 4) mixed-criticality scheduling that can pre-empt learning to protect real-time medical alerts, 5) online SMT-based runtime verification producing machine-checkable artefacts, or 6) privacy-preserving generative replay that stores zero latent tokens. All of these are new axes for continual learning.  Previous works cover sparsity, compute budgets, Bayesian uncertainty, graph memories or structural plasticity, but none integrate formal safety, carbon accounting and endurance into a single CL framework for wearable swarms.  The H-WIDE envelope and CarbIC market are conceptually novel, and the combination of these six axes represents a qualitative leap rather than an incremental tweak.
evaluate.significance_reason: If realised, SAFE-Swarm could enable continual learning on large populations of medical or AR wearables that are today barred by safety-certification, battery wear and upcoming eco-design regulations.  By guaranteeing zero overflow, <0.3 % missed alarms, 28 % grid-CO₂ reduction and 4.8× Flash lifetime, it addresses real industrial pain-points (regulatory compliance, carbon reporting, device longevity).  The formal proofs and per-trace monitoring raise the TRL for deploying CL in safety-critical domains, while private generative replay eliminates persistent personal data, answering privacy legislation.  Academically, it opens new research directions at the intersection of CL, real-time systems, sustainability and formal methods.  The main risk is engineering complexity, but the potential impact on healthcare, consumer IoT and carbon footprint is large.

idea.open_problems: 1. Existing SAFE-Swarm assumes that the *distribution* of worst-case tasks is known up–front; a single adversarially long tail task can still blow up any analytic envelope. 2. H-WIDE derives per-node bounds but does not *learn* from the fleet’s on-line traces – forcing designers to hand-tune budgets for every new hardware SKU. 3. PASS’s MILP scheduler scales poorly beyond ~150 real-time threads and ignores DMA/interrupt jitter that dominates latencies on cheap MCUs. 4. CarbIC accounts for grid CO₂ but not *battery embodied* carbon and ignores second-life scenarios (e-waste regulations now require reporting residual capacity). 5. PGR removes stored data yet keeps the UNet weights in Flash; over very long horizons these weights themselves dominate writes and carbon. 6. Safety proofs remain per-device; regulators increasingly demand *system­-of-systems* evidence across cooperative devices and cloud assist. 7. Public benchmarks still miss emergent sensor modalities (piezoresistive skins, mm-wave) and do not capture chronic usage (≥1 year) or second-owner transfer.
idea.methods:
We propose SAFE-Swarm 2.0 with four architecturally new pillars on top of the previous A–F stack.

G. Continual Envelope Meta-Learning (CEML)  
  • A Bayesian meta-learner updates the WC-TBE hyper-parameters online from fleet-wide traces using Thompson-constrained posterior sampling, tightening envelopes by up to 35 % while guaranteeing ≤10⁻⁶ under-estimation risk.

H. Real-time Probabilistic Scheduler (RT-PS)  
  • Replaces PASS MILP with an async server-less probabilistic reservation scheme based on Conditional Bernstein Bounds and queue-kicking, scaling to 10³ tasks with O(log n) updates and provably ≤1 µs jitter on Cortex-M33.

I. Life-Cycle Carbon & End-of-Life Optimiser (LiCCEL)  
  • Augments CarbIC with embedded-carbon tracking (mining, transport, re-manufacture).  Tokens become tri-dimensional ⟨Joules, gCO₂eq, SoH⟩; a multi-objective primal-dual solver maximises accuracy under Pareto-optimal life-cycle impact.

J. Flash-Zero Continual Weights (FZ-CW)  
  • Moves UNet + adapter weights into *Ferroelectric RAM* (MB85RS) banks exploited as cold-start overlays.  A group-testing Reed-Solomon scheme periodically reconstructs corrupted sectors, cutting cumulative Flash writes by 99 %.

K. System-level Formal Evidence (SYS-FE)  
  • Extends FRVL: model-checks the *entire* swarm–edge–cloud trace in TLA⁺, emits STARK proofs that any trace is envelope-conformant.  Proof size grows logarithmically with trace length (Succinctness theorem).

L. Chronic-Wear Benchmark Suite (CWB-365)  
  • 12-month sensor dump with RGB, IMU, mm-wave, piezo-skin, ECG, 150 tasks, two human subject cohorts incl. device hand-over at month-8.  Ships real battery/temperature/SoH logs for 5 MCU families.
idea.experimental_setup:
Hardware: 200-node fleet – 40 nRF5340, 40 ESP32-S3, 40 Apollo4 Blue, 40 MSP432E, 40 Pixel 8.  10 nodes equipped with 8 Mbit FRAM daughterboards.
Streams: existing Wear3-Stream, SpikeWear-DVS-v2, PhysioEvent-ECG plus new CWB-365.
Baselines: original SAFE-Swarm, µBit-Thermostat, HOT-Swarm, FedAvg-cloud-compressed, SparCL-DER++.
Metrics added: envelope shrinkage %, cumulative embodied-carbon gCO₂eq, fleet-level STARK proof size & verification time, Flash-write count, scheduler jitter P99.
Study duration: 60 simulated days + accelerated ageing equivalent to 1 year (Arrhenius).
Ablations: disable CEML, replace RT-PS with PASS, drop FRAM overlay, disable SYS-FE.
idea.expected_result:
• CEML reduces per-node worst-case energy bound by 31 % median without violating any trace.
• RT-PS keeps P99 end-to-end latency <6 ms with 910 concurrent tasks (vs 47 ms for PASS).  
• LiCCEL lowers life-cycle gCO₂eq by 22 % and extends battery second-life value by 1.8×.
• FZ-CW cuts cumulative Flash writes from 0.9 TB to 8 GB per node; Flash-based nodes hit endurance wall at 14 months, FRAM nodes survive 10 years.
• SYS-FE STARK proofs verify in 0.4 s on Pixel 8; proof size 2.1 MB for 30-day trace.
• Overall carbon-weighted welfare gains +19 % over original SAFE-Swarm.
idea.expected_conclusion: SAFE-Swarm 2.0 turns continual learning from a per-device engineering exercise into a self-optimising, formally verifiable *fleet* that remains safe, low-carbon and Flash-wear-free throughout a product’s whole life-cycle.  By shrinking worst-case envelopes through online meta-learning, scaling real-time scheduling, internalising embodied-carbon, eliminating Flash writes and generating succinct system-wide proofs, it satisfies upcoming IEC 62304-2, EU Battery and Eco-Design acts.  The public CWB-365 benchmark will anchor reproducible long-horizon research and open the door to sustainable, certifiable lifelong learning in medical, AR and circular-economy IoT deployments.

evaluate.novelty_reason: SAFE-Swarm 2.0 departs from mainstream continual-learning research in three orthogonal ways that are not covered by the surveyed literature. (1) Scope shift: it treats continual learning as a fleet–wide, real-time safety-critical problem and introduces Continual Envelope Meta-Learning that shrinks per-device worst-case bounds online; none of the related works (SparCL, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, Bayesian-structural, etc.) model worst-case energy/latency envelopes or update them from field traces. (2) Memory medium innovation: Flash-Zero Continual Weights moves all weights to ferroelectric RAM and combines it with group-testing RS reconstruction to cut 99 % of Flash writes—existing memory-efficiency papers work at the tensor/gradient level but assume conventional Flash/DRAM hardware. (3) Sustainability & formal evidence stack: LiCCEL’s tri-dimensional ⟨J, gCO₂eq, SoH⟩ tokens, SYS-FE’s system-of-systems STARK proofs, and the 12-month CWB-365 benchmark introduce carbon-aware optimisation and machine-verifiable safety guarantees—features absent from prior CL work. These pillars collectively create a design/verification pipeline (envelope learning → probabilistic scheduler → carbon-aware optimisation → formal proof) that is not a straightforward extension of any referenced technique.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, the method opens new research axes: (a) meta-learning of worst-case resource envelopes; (b) hardware/medium-aware weight storage and repair; (c) coupling life-cycle carbon accounting with continual adaptation; (d) scalable STARK-based certification of learning swarms. Each axis can spawn independent research threads beyond forgetting mitigation. Societally, the proposal tackles two pressing gaps for edge-AI products: compliance with emerging safety (IEC 62304-2) and eco-design/battery regulations, and longevity of low-cost devices whose Flash endurance is currently a blocker. The reported 31 % envelope shrinkage, 99 % write reduction and 22 % life-cycle CO₂ cut, if reproducible on the public CWB-365 benchmark, translate into fewer field failures, extended device life and lower carbon footprint at scale. The inclusion of formal proofs and a year-long benchmark also enhances reproducibility and regulator trust, elevating the practical impact far above incremental accuracy gains.
